THE AUTHOR’S NOTE

A little about me

At 16, I chose Humanities. At 18, I moved to Economics Honours. At 20, I discovered Design. And somewhere along the way, I realised that no single lens is enough to understand a problem.

Economics taught me to think about incentives, trade-offs, and the bigger picture. I still love looking at things through an economic lens, but it’s just one of the many hats I wear. I enjoy bringing together different perspectives to understand a problem better.

  • Incentives
  • Trade-offs
  • The bigger picture

I started my journey as a UI/UX Designer at a fintech startup, where I became curious about more than just the product. I wanted to understand the people using it, the services around it, and the decisions shaping their experiences. That curiosity led me to NID, where I’m pursuing my Master’s in Strategic Design Management.

At NID, I’ve learnt to move beyond what’s written on paper. I enjoy going into the field, talking to people, observing things firsthand, and connecting the dots between behaviour, services, systems, and economics. I like seeing how things actually work, not just how they are supposed to work.

Along the way, I’ve led teams, built collaborations, and learnt that leading and managing are different. Managing brings structure and gets things done; leading creates direction and brings people together. I believe good work needs a balance of both.

Today

I enjoy looking at problems from different angles to understand what people need, how organisations work, and where things can be made better.

My aim is to turn these perspectives into practical strategies that create value for both people and organisations.

Brand strategy · Koo & Kie

Because a drink needs a cookie.

koo & kie is a cookie brand concept built to complete the drink in your hand. This study covers the market, the rivals, the strategy, the identity, the packaging and the launch.

Brand strategyTeam of 4Timeline · 1 week
✦✧
What ?Because drink needs a cookie.
Overview

One cookie. One missing pairing.

Challenge

A large biscuit market, a premium segment led by filled and cream biscuits, and no cookie built around the drink you have with it.

Approach

Seven steps, from reading the market to launching on shelves. The flow below is the order of this study.

Outcome

koo & kie: eight cookies paired with chai, coffee and herbal tea, a full identity, packs, social posts and a four-phase launch.

MarketSize and share
RivalsThree profiles
VisionMission and idea
4 PsMarketing mix
STPWho it is for
BrandIdentity and packs
LaunchFour phases
01 · The market

India eats biscuits. The premium end is where the room is.

Method · Market research

Market size

USD 8.7–8.9B2030 (expected)CAGR ~6.5–9.6%

02 · The competition

Three rivals, three ways to win a shelf.

Method · Competitor profiles
~22%Dark Fantasy · share of premium cookies
~70%Nutri Choice · share of premium digestives
~10%Oreo · share of premium cream biscuits

Dark Fantasy

Since 2010₹1,000 crore+ sales by 2025

About and history

Dark Fantasy, ITC’s premium cookie brand under Sunfeast, pioneered India’s center-filled cookie segment in 2010. It holds ~22% of the ₹3,067 crore premium cookie market, valued at ~₹675 crore (2020), and surpassed ₹1,000 crore in annual sales by 2025.

Nutri Choice

Health segment leader₹1,000 crore+ (FY22)

About and history

NutriChoice leads India’s health biscuit segment with a ~70% share of the premium digestive category and annual revenue exceeding ₹1,000 crore (FY 2022). Its parent company, Britannia, holds about 38% of the overall organized biscuit market.

Oreo

Since 2011₹270–280 crore

About and history

Oreo, launched in India by Mondelez in 2011, is a global sandwich cookie brand with strong recognition but a modest local share. It holds about 10% of India’s premium cream-biscuit segment, contributing roughly ₹270–280 crore in revenue. Parent company Mondelez India reported total revenues of ₹7,278 crore, with Oreo positioned as a key premium offering.

To add. Your takeaway on the gap these three leave open. The deck lists the profiles but does not state it.

03 · About and vision

Redefining indulgence, one sip-and-bite at a time.

“Redefining indulgence, one perfect sip-and-bite pairing at a time.”

To delight cookie lovers with a guilt-free, New York–style indulgence — thick, soft, and flavor-packed — offering a premium, elevated snacking experience without compromise.

We aim to reimagine the way people enjoy cookies by introducing thoughtfully crafted flavour pairings that complement every sip — from the boldness of coffee to the richness of wine or the comfort of chai — creating perfect drink-cookie moments of indulgence.

04 · The marketing mix

Four Ps, one idea.

Method · 4 Ps

Product

  • Premium, better-for-you cookies crafted to complement tea and coffee moments along with other drinks
  • Made with locally ground multigrain, whole wheat, jaggery and nuts for balanced indulgence
  • Artisanal and gourmet cookies
  • Designed to enhance beverages, not overpower them
  • A guilt-free, everyday luxury that completes every cup

Price

  • Price per cookie: ₹40, positioned as an accessible premium indulgence
  • Target audience: young, urban consumers seeking a gourmet yet guilt-free treat
  • Value justification: made with ragi, whole wheat, dark chocolate and natural sweeteners
  • Wholesale pack: 4 cookies at ₹150
  • D2C offer: 4-cookie pack at ₹150 with an 8–10% discount to drive repeat orders

Place

  • D2C: website and hyperlocal sales for storytelling and subscriptions
  • B2B: café and corporate tie-ups for impulse sales
  • Retail: premium supermarkets and health stores in metros
  • Experiential: kiosks and pop-ups for tasting and brand engagement

Promotion

  • Core message: from snack to perfect pairing with better-for-you ingredients
  • Digital: Reels/Shorts showing texture, dunking and packaging
  • POS: table tents and signs suggesting pairings
  • Experiential: “Pairing Sessions” with coffee and tea brands

06 · Segmentation, targeting, positioning

Who it is for, and what it stands for.

Method · STP
The marketBiscuits and cookies in India

S

Segmentation

D2C psychographic
The Coffee Connoisseur

Primary D2C, values authenticity, functional pairing, brewing ritual extension. Influenced by expert reviews.

The Urban Entertainer

High AOV, uses food to signal status, driven by gifting aesthetics and unique flavor stories.

The Mindful Indulger

Secondary volume, seeks control (less sweet, high fiber), appreciates portion control.

B2B geographic / channel
National Specialty Coffee Chains

Core B2B in Tier-1 metros, require centralized logistics and a high-margin model.

Premium Ancillary Retail

High-end co-working, boutique hotels, gourmet food halls; need individual, tamper-proof, high-status packaging.

T

Targeting

Primary D2C target

The Ritualist

Urban millennial30–45
  • Profile: sees daily specialty coffee or cold brew as a non-negotiable ritual.
  • Need: the cookie must enhance the primary beverage; drives subscriptions for Coffee and Cold Brew pairing lines.
Primary B2B target

The Specialty Chain Partner

Operations / procurement headse.g. Blue Tokai, Subko
  • Need: a zero-headache supplier for a unique, branded SKU with 50%+ profit margin; drives national contracts.
P

Positioning

  • Core position: expert authority on beverage accompaniment; moving from a simple cookie to an essential, engineered food product.
  • Statement: “koo & kie is the single-portion, chunky New York-style cookie… scientifically designed to complete every sip, from specialty coffees to fine wines.”
Key pillars
High indulgence and high functional specialization

Chunky, XL size plus flavor engineering for purpose-driven fillings.

“Not too sweet”

Catering to the sophisticated Indian palate.

07 · Point of differentiation

Why people would pick it, from their side of the table.

  1. Engineered beverage pairing

    Guarantees the perfect cookie for every drink.

    Consumer benefitNo more guessing which cookie goes best!

  2. Sophisticated “not too sweet” flavour profile

    Refined taste, never cloyingly sweet, for discerning palates.

    Consumer benefitIndulgence feels guilt-free and truly premium.

  3. Curated, high-end ritual enhancement

    Transforms daily pauses into accessible luxury moments.

    Consumer benefitPortion control // experience sophistication with every bite.

  4. Health-conscious, transparent ingredients

    Superior atta and ragi for a demonstrably healthier choice.

    Consumer benefitA healthier, higher-quality choice.

Design research · Wellness tourism in India

Making Indian wellness easy to choose and trust

A framework and information layer that turns India’s fragmented wellness market into a clear, verifiable decision journey for travellers.

Design ResearchService DesignSystems MappingStakeholder AnalysisJourney MappingFramework DesignWellness Tourism

India is the origin of Ayurveda, the birthplace of yoga, and holds over 5,000 years of healing wisdom.

A traveller abroad wants the kind of healing India has practised for over 5,000 years. Then they try to pick a centre, and the trust runs out somewhere between the search bar and the booking button. This project asks why, and what a clearer journey could change.

Design researchTeam of 3 · Anamika, Navisha Rai, Sanchi SikkaStrategic Design Management, NID
A project forGujarat TourismResearch on wellness tourism in India, done with the Gujarat Tourism team.
$1.3TGlobal wellness tourism market, and growing
7–8%India’s share, against a 13% global average
41–53%More spent by international wellness travellers than the average tourist
0.34India’s system maturity score. Peer nations sit between 0.92 and 1.00
The story in six steps
  1. 1The promise5,000 years of healing, yet only 7–8% of wellness tourism
  2. 2The questionWhat problems do people face during their wellness journey?
  3. 3The listeningInterviews, scenarios, client visits and enquiries
  4. 4The patternSix phases of choosing, and a gap in every one
  5. 5The insightThe problem lies in discovery and decision making
  6. 6The answerA shared language and information layers, tested with 20 people
Overview

The problem was never availability.

Challenge

India is the birthplace of yoga and Ayurveda, yet it captures only 7–8% of wellness tourism. Almost half of what it should.

Approach

We benchmarked global standards, then spoke to retreat-goers, government bodies, centres and trip planners, and visited centres as clients ourselves.

Outcome

A design direction built on four moves, and information layers that make treatments legible. We tested it with 20 people.

India’s share, against the global average

India7–8%
Global average13%
Bars are scaled to the 13% global average
01 · Understanding the context

Let’s begin with what wellness tourism in India actually is.

Travel where the main goal is to improve physical, mental and spiritual wellbeing, through indigenous practices and nature-based experiences.

41%

International wellness travellers spend 41% to 53% more than average international tourists.

Wellness tourism in India often overlaps with:

01 · Ayurveda retreats
  • Detox (Panchakarma)
  • Herbal treatments
  • Diet-based healing
02 · Yoga and meditation
  • Daily yoga routines
  • Breathwork (pranayama)
  • Silent retreats
01 · Nature based healing
  • Forest stays
  • Eco-retreats
  • Mountain or coastal healing environments
02 · Spiritual wellness
  • Ashram living
  • Guided introspection
  • Mindfulness practices

So we asked: which system is already working?

We looked at medical tourism. Its structured, trust-driven approach makes the journey clear from first search to follow-up. In wellness tourism in India, that customer journey is still missing.

Then we benchmarked wellness standards across countries.

Method · Global benchmarking

Despite a wellness market worth over $15 billion, India is one of the only countries in the comparison without a mandatory national accreditation system, a structured pre-visit health consultation, or a unified digital health record for international users.

India0.34
USA0.94
Germany1.00
China0.92
Japan0.98
UK0.96
Accreditation & standardsPatient journey standardsTourist-facing communication

The offerings are strong. The system around the journey is fragmented, so it is hard for people to discover, trust and decide.

02 · Research framing & primary research

How we converged on one question.

Story so far. The promise is clear: five thousand years of healing, and only 7–8% of the market. So the question became what goes wrong between wanting a retreat in India and booking one.

How we proceeded
to converge

What are the problems people face during their wellness journey?

Our tool

Case-based scenario

Our tool

Participatory experience audit

In the field

Making sense of it: four ways of synthesising.

Method · Affinity mapping, pattern analysis, root cause analysis

Data synthesis

01 · Pattern analysis
  • Identify recurring themes
  • Common behaviours across users, stakeholders and systems
  • Observations to structured insights
02 · Quantification of patterns
  • Mapping and comparing patterns
  • Understanding their frequency and significance across the journey
  • Prioritising critical gaps that affect user experience and decision-making
03 · Stakeholder misalignment
  • Different stakeholders perceive and interact with the system differently (users, providers, government, intermediaries)
  • Expectations, communication and service delivery revealed key disconnects
04 · Root cause analysis of the patterns
  • Traced the identified gaps
  • Discovered the underlying systemic causes
  • Causal mapping of the various insights

From primary research, one thing was clear. The problem lies in discovery and decision making.

Research instrument

The questions guide.

One shared question, four groups of people. The prompts are organised by the stage of the journey they were meant to uncover.

Method · Interviews
  1. Trigger

    What made you start looking for a wellness retreat, and what did you compare India against?

  2. Validation

    How did you decide that India was the right destination for what you wanted?

  3. Selection

    How did you shortlist centres? What did you look for, and what could you not find?

  4. Evaluation

    How did you work out what each treatment was, and whether it was right for you?

  5. Trust and safety

    What made you trust, or doubt, a centre before you arrived? Did you check any accreditation?

  6. Booking

    What were you asked before booking, and how did the stay compare with what you expected?

Method · Interviews
  1. Definition

    How does your framework define wellness, and how is it different from a hospital or a spa?

  2. Accreditation

    What accreditation exists for wellness centres, and who verifies it?

  3. Visibility

    How is accreditation shown to travellers, especially international ones?

  4. Regulation

    Who regulates the wellness market today, and where are the gaps?

Method · Inquiry, as clients
  1. Recommendation

    What would you recommend for someone who wants stress relief or better sleep, and why?

  2. Consultation

    Is a doctor consultation or medical intake part of the booking?

  3. Language

    How do you explain the treatment names to a first-time visitor?

  4. Proof

    Can I see practitioner qualifications, accreditation or outcomes before I book?

Method · Case-based scenario
  1. Set-up

    You are planning a wellness trip to India. Here are the options. Which one do you choose?

  2. Reasoning

    What made you choose it, and what would have changed your mind?

  3. Information

    What else would you want to know before booking?

03 · Pattern making

Six phases of choosing, and a gap in every one.

Story so far. The research gave us stories. We lined them up along the traveller’s path, from first idea to booking, to see exactly where the journey breaks.

We mapped how an international traveller moves from first idea to booking, and set it against what India’s centres actually offer at each step.

Five major gaps

  1. DiscoveryScattered information around the wellness industry
  2. ClarityNo standardisation of services or terminology
  3. TrustWeak certification visibility and safety signalling
  4. PersonalisationNo diagnosis before a treatment is purchased
  5. SystemicA fragmented, non-integrated user journey
04 · Pattern analysis

What weighed most on people’s decisions.

Story so far. Not every gap weighs the same. We scored what mattered most to decisions, then read each interview note by how the experience felt and how much trust it built.

Lack of transparency in communication

Hidden costs and rules that surface on-site damage trust in the centre’s digital presence after the fact. The website starts to feel like a curated front, not a truthful preview.

10/10
Critical

Validation from multiple sources

Users cross-check YouTube, Instagram and reviews to build their own picture of trust. With formal credentials unknown, they lean on visual proxies: clean spaces, campus photos, smiling staff.

10/10
Critical

Word of mouth prevalence

Even after research across channels, the final decision is anchored to someone they trust. The gut feeling that closes the loop is almost always social, not informational.

7/10
Elevated

People did not check for accreditation

Centre websites rarely show Ayush or NABH status, and users don’t know to look for it. So the visit reinforces not knowing.

10/10
Critical
72%of the research cohort used the website as their primary digital touchpoint
8/10Visual authenticity. A professional-looking interface correlates strongly with trust

Stakeholders
misalignment mapping

Reading the gaps through a service-quality lens

Model · SERVQUAL, five dimensions of service quality

SERVQUAL describes service quality in five parts. Set against it, each of our findings lands in one dimension, and none of them sits in the centre yet.

  • ReliabilityNo standard outcome disclosure, and inconsistent trust across centres
  • AssuranceNo visible accreditation, trust mark or practitioner qualifications
  • TangiblesUsers lean on visual proxies: clean spaces, campus photos, smiling staff
  • EmpathyNo diagnosis before a treatment is purchased
  • ResponsivenessMedical queries go unresolved, with no pre-visit consultation

Draft mapping. Which finding sits under which dimension is our reading; adjust it if your team reads it differently.

05 · Insight framing

Diving below the iceberg.

Story so far. Patterns tell us what happens. Insights tell us why. We went one level deeper, to the causes underneath.

Once the patterns were visible, we looked underneath them. Six insights came out.

Method · Root cause analysis, iceberg model
Insight 01

Ayurveda as aftercare, not preventive care

Not used in emergency careNot part of daily preventive behaviourTurned to after failure or fatigue from other treatmentsAdoption concentrated in the 40–49 age group

Traditional wellness

Diagnosis-led

Adaptive to each person

Practitioner-guided

Commercial wellness

Standardised packages

Scalability-first

Product-led

The mismatch between the two leads to consumer confusion
Insight 03

Stuck between clinically credible and commercially appealing

Clinical · hospitalWellness centresCommercial · resort
Calls itself a “hospital” to gain credibilityMarkets as a “retreat” to attract touristsTrust is inconsistent across centres

Oral traditionKnowledge passed through lineage, not text
Variable protocolsEach practitioner follows their own judgement
No outcome metricsFew ways to measure what worked
No structured documentation: outcomes are invisible and unverifiable
Trust and credibility cannot be built

06 · Solution framing

Now that we understood the gaps, what could actually improve the experience?

Story so far. Six insights pointed the same way: people struggle to discover, trust and decide because the information layer is missing. That is where we chose to work.

Design considerations

Three systems have to work together for wellness to thrive: the socio-economic context, the natural environment, and the healthcare ecosystem. This is the GWI model for a thriving economy.

Model · GWI (Global Wellness Institute) model

Design direction: four moves toward a way forward

We chose to work in Communicate: standardising the information layer people use to decide.

Defining wellness in India

Everything starts with a shared language. A four-dimension framework gives centres, travellers and government the same way to describe what a wellness offering is.

  1. 1Primary framework structure
    • Intent
    • System of care
    • Mode of delivery
    • Outcome orientation
    • Evidence & transparency
  2. 2Dimension 1 · Intent (why)
    • Preventive
    • Curative
    • Restorative
    • Transformative
    • Lifestyle
  3. 3Dimension 2 · System of care (what)
    • Ayurveda
    • Yoga
    • Meditation
    • Naturopathy
    • Integrative
  4. 4Dimension 3 · Mode of delivery (how)
    • Feeling calmer
    • Physiological
    • Better sleep
    • Clinical
    • Spiritual sense of meaning
  5. 5Dimension 4 · Outcome orientation
    • Subjective
    • Physiological
    • Behavioural
    • Clinical
    • Spiritual
SCREEN TO ADDYour screen or poster: the four-dimension framework

An outcome measurement tool, so results can be seen

Today’s tools are clinically meaningful, but methodologically weak and inconsistently used.

Different questionnaires give different results for the same person.
Two practitioners may assess the same person differently.
Self-perception questions (“Do you have good digestion?”) and vague terms (“often”, “sometimes”).
Few tools are tested for reliability, construct validity or correlation with biomarkers.
Prakriti and Vikriti are not kept separate.
Prakriti

An individual’s innate, unchanging natural constitution (genetic makeup).

Vikriti

The current state of imbalance or illness.

Measure vikriti from the patient’s side to give outcome evidence.

08 · Validation & impact

Did it land with real people?

Story so far. The last chapter of the story: put it in front of people and see whether choosing gets easier.

PHOTO TO ADDYour photo: testing the concepts with 20 people
75%

We tested the concepts with 20 people. 15 of them liked the idea and said it would make choosing a wellness centre in India easier.

15 of 20 people · 75% said yes

What this could change

For the traveller

Understand what a treatment is, who it’s for and what to expect, before committing time and money.

For centres

A common language and visible credentials, so they are chosen on merit and not on photographs.

For India

A trusted, shared story of wellness that helps close the gap between 7–8% and the 13% global average.
